newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. April trade gap $8.36 bln.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. April trade gap $8.36 bln.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the U.S. trade gap widened to $8.36 billion from a revised $7.76 billion gap in March.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a $10.0 billion trade deficit.
RICHARD KOSS, ECONOMIST, MARIA FIORINI RAMIREZ, INC: "It's actually a bit smaller than what people expected in terms of the deficit, which in that sense is beter."
"It appears as though that some of the special factors that people were looking for to come off, like the aircraft, didn't retreat as much as people were looking for.
"That said, the one element here that I think it's pretty good is the notion of continuing strength in exports of capital goods out of the U.S."

JOSH FEINMAN, GLOBAL MARKETS ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST CO: "A little smaller deficit than expected, especially with the revisions, and that will provide a boost to first quarter GDP. In other words, trade will be less a drain than originally thought.

"I think it could push first quarter GDP up a few tenths, so we might get over six percent. And in the second quarter I think trade is likely to be a bit of an add, the net export sector, because you now have an average montly deficit in Q1 of $10 billion and April with $8.5 billion, so the second quarter is likely to be smaller.
"I'm still sticking with a call of GDP growth of about one and a half in the second quarter."
LYNN REASER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BARNETT BANK INC: "Exports are showing considerable strength, which is particularly good news in the face of a strong dollar.
"It indicates the improvement in various countries throughout the world and that U.S productivity is allowing good export performance."

SAMUEL KAHAN, PRESIDENT, A.S.K. FINANCIAL RESEARCH LTD: "Most people were looking for it to widen out to $9.0 billion or $10.0 billion. The increase in imports was not that great and that's what kept the trade deficit from widening out as much as expected.
"The surpise was that exports, instead of declining, actually rose.
"Because the trade balance is not as narrow as it was before, it strengthens second-quarter GDP."
